newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin euro scheme generates interest, weak sales.
newsitem.headline: Berlin euro scheme generates interest, weak sales.

text.p: A 10-day trial to win Berliners over to the planned European single currency was a limited success, its sponsors said Monday, admitting that few seemed willing to trade their beloved marks for euros.

Officials from participating shops and banks and the Berlin delegation of the European Commission said the German capital reacted to the special-issue euros with equal measures of curiosity and distrust during the short test-run which ended on Sunday.
"I would rather not say what sales were like during this Euro Week," said Petula Hassert, manager of the Kaufhof am Alex department store in east Berlin. "Let's just say they were really mediocre."
The Kaufhof am Alex had constructed a small display decorated with blue and gold European flags, offering 25 kitchen products that customers could buy with euros or marks.
Hassert said consumers needed more facts about the currency before they would be ready to begin using it for shopping.

"I think having information stands available for people visiting our store would have been a much better idea," Hassert said. "Our customers did seem quite interested in the euro and we had fun with it, but it didn't materialise into sales."

A spokeswoman for luxury department store Kaufhaus des Westens (KaDeWe) in western Berlin described turnover during the euro trial as slow and estimated the store had taken in about 100 euros per day on wares available for the currency.

A LandesBank Berlin spokesman said it was pleased with the public response to the trial, estimating it had distributed over 500,000 euros at its 250 branch offices and outdoor euro stands during the course of the programme.

The bank manufactured 1.3 million special coins for use at an exchange rate of two marks to one euro during the trial in denominations of 1.5 euros (three marks), 2.5 euros (five marks), and 10 euros (20 marks).
Germans have developed deep faith in the mark during its 49-year history, seeing its strength as the bedrock of the country's post-war prosperity and stability.
Leading German consumer body Verbraucherzentrale reported this month that over 60 percent of Germans remain sceptical about the euro and feel unwilling to trade the mark for it.
European Commission organisers of the project considered tempering such fears of the euro as the primary goal of the trial.

"One recognises that this project is controversial," said Eckhard Jaedtke, head of the Berlin delegation to the European Commission, adding that Germans should not see the introduction of the euro as synonymous with having a weaker currency.
Jaedtke called the euro campaign successful in drumming up the interest of the public and the press, which he said could only help the forward march of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"We had never had the chance to communicate with so many people about the euro," Jaedtke said. "(The trial) was a success because it put the euro in people's hands, making the whole idea tangible."

The Berlin euro scheme was not the first of its kind in Germany. Last October, a similar programme in the Black Forest town of Waldkirch also failed to live up to expectations when Germans proved to be more interested in keeping the coins than in spending them.
If EMU is implemented on schedule, citizens in participating countries will see their national currencies phased out between January and July 2002 and replaced with the euro.
Before then, more euro trials are planned in Germany and throughout Europe, organisers of the Berlin programme said,
